subject: History
description: Mughal zabti, Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari, Mahalwari — architects and provinces

questions.stem: The 'Zabti' (or 'Dahsala') system of Mughal land revenue — based on measured area and a 10-year price average — is credited to:
questions.explanation: Todar Mal, Akbar's revenue minister (Diwan-i-Ashraf / Diwan-i-Kul), introduced the Dahsala system in 1580. Land was surveyed, classified into four types — Polaj (always cultivated), Parauti (fallow one year), Chachar (fallow 3-4 years), Banjar (fallow >5 years). A 10-year average of produce and prices was fixed; revenue = 1/3 of the average. Sher Shah had earlier made the measurement-based assessments that Todar Mal refined.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Permanent Settlement of 1793 in Bengal was introduced by:
questions.explanation: Lord Cornwallis (Governor-General 1786-93) introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal, Bihar, Orissa in 1793. Zamindars became owners of land; revenue was fixed in perpetuity. The drafters were John Shore and James Grant. The 'sunset clause' said zamindars who failed to pay by sunset on the due date lost their estates. Criticism — fixed revenue benefited zamindars (prices rose, peasants suffered); led to mass transfer of land to city-based moneylenders.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Ryotwari system — assessing revenue directly from the cultivator — was introduced primarily in Madras and Bombay Presidencies by:
questions.explanation: The Ryotwari system (ryot = peasant) eliminated middlemen — direct link between the state and the cultivator. Alexander Read piloted it in the Baramahal (1792) and Thomas Munro extended it across Madras Presidency after becoming Governor (1820). Also adopted by Bombay under Elphinstone and in parts of Assam. Revenue was usually 45-55% of the produce; re-assessed every 20-30 years. Peasant retained ownership but bore all risk.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Mahalwari system — where revenue was assessed on a 'mahal' (village / estate group) collectively — was introduced in:

options.option_text: North-Western Provinces, Punjab and parts of Central India

questions.explanation: Mahalwari — formalised by Holt Mackenzie's 1822 Regulation VII and revised by R.M. Bird's 1833 settlement — covered the North-Western Provinces (modern UP), Punjab (after 1849 annexation), parts of the Central Provinces (modern MP). Revenue fixed on the entire mahal; the village headman (lambardar) collected from cultivators and paid the state. Revision every 20-30 years. Combined features of both Zamindari and Ryotwari.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Under the Permanent Settlement, the share of revenue demanded from the zamindar was approximately:
questions.explanation: Zamindar paid 10/11 to the Company; kept 1/11 as remuneration. Revenue was fixed in 1793 at a very high level (on inflated 1789 prices) — in the next decade, two-fifths of Bengal's zamindars defaulted and their estates were auctioned. Buyers were often Calcutta merchants / officials — creating a new class of absentee landlords. The 'famous' (or infamous) Sunset Law drove the auction process.

questions.stem: The 'Jagirdari' and 'Mansabdari' systems of Mughal administration were closely linked because:

options.option_text: Mansabdars received land in lieu of salary
Jagirs were reserved only for the royal family
Mansab ranks were purchased, not assigned
Jagirdars were exempt from military service

questions.explanation: A mansabdar held a 'mansab' (rank) with two numbers — zat (personal rank) and sawar (cavalry he maintained). Salary could be paid in cash (naqdi) or by assignment of a jagir — the right to collect revenue from a specified area. Most mansabdars were jagirdars. Jagirs were transferable and non-hereditary — part of Akbar's centralising design. Highest zat was reserved for princes; nobles went up to 7,000/7,000.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: By the time of independence in 1947, the approximate share of Indian territory under each British revenue system was:
questions.explanation: By 1947, Zamindari (Permanent Settlement + temporary zamindari variants) covered ~57% of cultivated land — chiefly Bengal, Bihar, eastern UP, parts of Madras and Central Provinces. Ryotwari was ~38% — Madras, Bombay, Assam, Berar. Mahalwari was ~5% — parts of UP, Punjab, Central India. Post-1947 Zamindari Abolition Acts (1950 onwards) dismantled intermediaries; state-level tenancy reforms followed.
